analogy.p: Imagine water falling down a pipe onto a turbine. The height the water falls is like the potential difference (energy per unit of water), and the amount of water passing per second is like the current. The power delivered to the turbine is the energy each kilogram of water gives up multiplied by the number of kilograms per second, which maps to P = V x I. Double the flow rate or double the height and you get double the power. The analogy breaks down because real electrons do not 'fall' and the P = I²R heating comes from collisions with ions, which a water pipe does not show well; also charge is not used up in a circuit, while water leaves the bottom of the pipe.
analogy.t: Water flowing through a hydroelectric turbine

bullets: Power = energy transferred / time, P = E / t, where P is in watts (W), E in joules (J) and t in seconds (s).
Equivalently power = work done / time, P = W / t, because work done is energy transferred.
One **watt** is a rate of transfer of one joule per second: 1 W = 1 J/s.
A device rated at 100 W transfers 100 J of energy every second it is operating.
Power is a rate, so it is never 'used up': energy is transferred (electrically to thermal, kinetic, light and sound), and power is how quickly that happens.
Power is a scalar quantity: it has size but no direction.
Link to Energy topic: the rate of energy transfer is also what efficiency compares (useful power out / total power in).
core.h: Power: the idea and the definition
core.p: **Power** is the rate at which energy is transferred, or the rate at which work is done. A high-power device transfers a lot of energy every second; a low-power device transfers only a little. This is why a 3 kW kettle boils water quickly while a 5 W phone charger barely warms up. Power does not tell you the total energy that has been transferred (that also depends on how long the device is on); it only tells you how fast the transfer is happening.

bullets: P = V I: power (W) = potential difference (V) x current (A).
P = I²R: power (W) = (current)² (A²) x resistance (ohm).
Rearrangements of P = VI: I = P / V and V = P / I.
Rearrangements of P = I²R: R = P / I² and I = square root of (P / R).
Both equations are given for the power transferred by any circuit device; for a resistor or heater this energy is transferred as thermal energy.
Learn both equations (and P = E / t) as you may be expected to recall them rather than be given them.
Always show the equation, the substitution with units, and the final answer with units; that is how method marks are earned.
core.h: The two electrical power equations you must recall
core.p: In circuits, power can be linked to the potential difference across a device and the current through it. The AQA equation list gives you two equations that must be recalled: **power = potential difference x current (P = VI)** and **power = current squared x resistance (P = I²R)**. Both describe the same physical idea. Choose the one that matches the information in the question: if you are told V and I use P = VI, and if you are told I and R use P = I²R.

bullets: V = E / Q means 1 volt = 1 joule per coulomb.
I = Q / t means 1 ampere = 1 coulomb per second.
V x I = (E / Q) x (Q / t) = E / t = P, because the charge Q cancels.
Units check: volt x ampere = (J/C) x (C/s) = J/s = watt.
For a fixed potential difference, a bigger current means more charge passing per second, so more energy per second is transferred.
For a fixed current, a bigger potential difference means each coulomb transfers more energy, so power is greater.
This is why mains appliances that need a large power, such as kettles and heaters, draw a large current at 230 V.
core.p: Potential difference is the energy transferred per unit charge (V = E / Q) and current is the charge flowing per second (I = Q / t). Multiply the energy per coulomb by the number of coulombs per second and you get the energy per second, which is power. So P = VI is really the definition of power, rewritten in electrical quantities. This is a great way to remember the equation and also a good explanation for a 'why' question.

bullets: Start: P = V I.
Ohm's law: V = I R.
Substitute: P = I x (I R) = I x I x R = I²R.
Substituting the other way (I = V / R) gives P = V²/R, a useful alternative when V and R are known (you can use it if you derive it, but P = VI and P = I²R are the equations to recall).
Because of the square, doubling the current multiplies the power by 4 (if R is constant); trebling the current multiplies it by 9; halving it divides the power by 4.
A common error is writing P = IR²; the current is squared, not the resistance.
You may be asked to show or use this derivation in a 'show that' or 'explain' question.
core.h: Deriving P = I²R from P = VI and V = IR
core.p: The second equation is not a new law; it comes from combining P = VI with Ohm's law V = IR. Substitute IR in place of V and the power becomes I x (I R), which is I²R. This is useful when you know the current and the resistance but not the potential difference, for example the heating in a wire. It also shows that the power dissipated in a resistor depends on the **square** of the current.

bullets: 1 kilowatt (kW) = 1000 W, so 2.3 kW = 2300 W.
1 megawatt (MW) = 1 000 000 W; a power station may output hundreds of MW.
1 milliwatt (mW) = 0.001 W.
1 milliampere (mA) = 0.001 A, so 250 mA = 0.25 A.
Time must be in seconds for E = Pt; in P = E/t, minutes must be x60 and hours x3600.
Standard form helps with big and small values, for example 1.5 MW = 1.5 x 10^6 W.
A kilowatt-hour (kWh) is a unit of energy, not power; do not confuse kW and kWh (see the energy-transfer note).
core.p: Power is measured in **watts (W)**, but real appliances have powers that are very small or very large, so prefixes are common. Check the units before substituting into any equation: the equations only work in W, V, A, ohm, J and s. Marks are regularly lost by leaving a power in kW or a current in mA when substituting.

bullets: **E = P x t**: a 2000 W heater running for 60 s transfers 120 000 J.
**P = E / t**: the same energy transferred in half the time needs twice the power.
**t = E / P**: use this to find how long a device takes to transfer a given amount of energy.
1 W = **1 joule per second** (1 J/s), which is how the watt is defined.
Convert time to seconds: **1 minute = 60 s, 1 hour = 3600 s**.
Convert power to watts: **1 kW = 1000 W**, 1 MW = 1 000 000 W.
E = VIt follows by substituting P = VI, linking energy to potential difference, current and time.
Check the units: **W x s = J**; if you get kJ or kWh, convert before comparing.
core.h: Power, energy and time: E = Pt
core.p: Because power is the rate of energy transfer, the energy transferred is found by multiplying power by time: **energy transferred = power x time (E = Pt)**, with energy in joules (J), power in watts (W) and time in seconds (s). Rearranged, **P = E / t** and **t = E / P**. Combining this with P = VI shows that the energy transferred by an electrical device is E = VIt. Always convert minutes and hours into seconds before using the equation, because 1 W is exactly 1 J per second.

bullets: Electrons gain kinetic energy from the cell/supply and transfer it to the lattice ions during collisions.
The rate of this energy transfer is the power P = I²R, so it grows with the square of the current.
A higher resistance wire transfers more power for the same current, which is why heating elements are made of high-resistance wire (nichrome).
Useful heating: kettles, toasters, electric fires, immersion heaters.
Unwanted heating: wires in cables, computers and phone chargers get warm; this wasted energy is dissipated to the surroundings.
Overheating risk: if current is too large the wire becomes very hot, so a fuse is used to break the circuit.
Link to Resistance topic: a filament lamp's resistance increases as it heats, because the lattice ions vibrate more and electrons collide more often.
core.h: The heating effect of a current and why I²R matters
core.p: When a current flows through a resistor, the charge carriers (free electrons in a metal) collide with the ions of the lattice. In each collision energy is transferred to the ions, which vibrate more, so the thermal energy store of the resistor increases and its temperature rises. The greater the current, the more collisions per second and the harder the collisions, so the heating effect grows faster than the current. This is exactly what P = I²R says. The energy is then dissipated to the surroundings.

bullets: UK mains supply is about 230 V (alternating, 50 Hz).
Approximate typical ratings (they vary by model): LED lamp about 8 W, phone charger about 5 to 20 W, TV about 100 W, toaster about 1 kW, kettle about 2 to 3 kW.
Normal current = rated power / mains voltage, for example 1150 W / 230 V = 5.0 A.
Rated power is only true if the appliance is connected to the correct potential difference.
Appliances with a heating element have much larger powers than those that only run electronics.
Total power of several appliances on one circuit adds up: P total = P1 + P2 + P3, so their currents add too.
Extension leads can overheat if too many high-power devices are plugged in, because the total current is large.
core.h: Rated power and what it means on an appliance
core.p: Every mains appliance has a rating plate stating a **rated voltage** (230 V in the UK) and a **rated power**. The rated power tells you how many joules per second the appliance transfers when it is working normally. You can use P = VI to work out the normal current it draws from the mains: I = P / V. Higher rated power means a larger current from the supply, so thicker cable and a bigger fuse may be needed.

bullets: Step 1: convert the power to watts.
Step 2: I = P / V with V = 230 V.
Step 3: choose the next rating above the current (3 A, 5 A or 13 A).
A 3 A fuse is suitable for appliances up to 3 x 230 = 690 W.
A 5 A fuse is suitable up to 5 x 230 = 1150 W.
A 13 A fuse is suitable up to 13 x 230 = 2990 W; most high-power appliances use this.
Fuse in the live wire: if a fault makes too much current flow, the fuse melts and the appliance is isolated from the live supply.
Exam wording: 'the fuse melts because the current is greater than its rating, which breaks the circuit'.
core.h: Choosing a fuse using P = VI
core.p: A **fuse** contains a thin wire that heats up and melts if the current through it exceeds the fuse rating, breaking the circuit and protecting the appliance and cable. A fuse is placed in the live wire. Common values in a UK plug are 3 A, 5 A and 13 A. To choose a fuse, find the normal current with I = P / V, then select the **lowest standard fuse rating above this current**. If the fuse is too low it blows during normal use; if it is too high it will not protect the cable from overheating.

bullets: Series circuit: the current is the same everywhere, so the component with the largest resistance transfers the most power.
Parallel circuit: the potential difference is the same across each branch, so the branch with the smallest resistance has the largest current and the largest power.
Doubling V across a fixed resistor doubles I (Ohm's law) and so P = VI becomes 4 times bigger.
Doubling R at constant V halves I and so halves P.
A variable resistor in series reduces the current and so reduces the power transferred to a lamp or motor (dimmer effect).
In a lamp-and-resistor series circuit, the potential difference splits in the ratio of their resistances.
A filament lamp does not obey constant R, so P-V is not a parabola for it; use the measured V and I readings instead.
core.h: Resistance, current and power: how the variables interact
core.p: Whether more resistance means more or less power depends on what is being held constant, and examiners like students who notice this. If the same current flows (components in series), P = I²R says larger R gives larger P. If the same potential difference is across each component (components in parallel, like mains appliances), then P = V²/R says a larger R gives a smaller P. Always identify what is the same in the circuit before predicting.

bullets: For a given power transmitted, P = VI means higher V gives lower I.
Power wasted in the cables = I²R, so if I is reduced by a factor of 10 the wasted power falls by a factor of 100.
Step-up transformers raise V for transmission; step-down transformers lower it for safe use at homes (230 V).
Thick cables with low resistance, such as aluminium with a steel core, also reduce losses.
This is a classic 4 to 6 mark answer: link P = VI, then P = I²R, then reduced energy loss.
High voltage is dangerous, so cables are suspended on pylons or buried underground.
See the National Grid note for the full explanation.
core.h: Power loss in cables and the National Grid
core.p: The cables that carry electricity have a small resistance, and a current in them transfers wasted thermal energy at a rate P = I²R. Because the power lost depends on the square of the current, reducing the current massively reduces the energy wasted. The National Grid does this by using step-up transformers to raise the potential difference to 400 000 V, which lowers the current for the same transmitted power (P = VI) and so cuts the I²R losses.

bullets: Efficiency = useful power output / total power input.
Efficiency can never be greater than 1 (100 per cent) because energy is conserved.
Total power input of an electrical device is given by P = VI.
Example: a lamp with an input of 60 W and a useful light output of 6 W has efficiency 6 / 60 = 0.10 (10 per cent).
Reduce waste with thermal insulation, lubrication, and low-resistance wires.
LED lamps are much more efficient than filament lamps, so for the same light output they have a lower power rating.
Link to Energy topic: energy is conserved, never created or destroyed; it is dissipated.
core.p: Efficiency compares the useful power output with the total power input: efficiency = useful power output / total power input (as a decimal or a percentage). A kettle is nearly 100 per cent efficient at transferring electrical energy to thermal energy, but a filament lamp is very inefficient because most of its power is transferred as heat rather than light. Wasted energy is dissipated to the surroundings, making them warmer.

bullets: Measure V with a voltmeter connected in parallel and I with an ammeter connected in series.
Calculate P = V x I for each reading; repeat and calculate a mean.
Graph of P (y-axis) against I (x-axis) is a curve through the origin (parabola).
Graph of P against I² is a straight line through the origin; the gradient equals R.
Graph of P against V is a curve for a fixed resistor; P against V² is a straight line with gradient 1/R.
Use significant figures consistent with the data and give units.
Sources of error: wires heating (resistance changes), meter zero errors, and reading errors from analogue meters.
Always check that a final power is sensible (for example, a kettle should be about kilowatts, not milliwatts).
core.h: Practical and data skills linked to power
core.p: You will often meet power in experiments and data tables. In the specific heat capacity required practical, an electrical heater is connected to a power supply, with an ammeter and a voltmeter, and the electrical power is found from P = VI. Multiplying by time gives the energy supplied (E = Pt). In graph questions, remember that power depends on the square of the current, so a P against I graph is a curve, whereas P against I² is a straight line through the origin with gradient R.

exam: Command words: 'State' = one fact; 'Calculate' = equation, substitution, answer and unit; 'Explain' = give a reason using linked ideas (because ... so ...).
A typical 2-mark calculation: 1 mark for the correct substitution (e.g. P = 230 x 10), 1 mark for the answer with unit (2300 W). Always write the equation first.
If the question gives I and R, use P = I²R; if it gives V and I, use P = VI; if it gives energy and time, use P = E / t.
Convert units before substituting (kW to W, mA to A, minutes to seconds). Showing the conversion earns the method mark even if the final value is wrong.
Fuse questions (usually 2 to 3 marks): calculate I = P / V, then state the fuse with the next value above the current; say that a lower fuse would blow in normal use.
'Explain why doubling the current quadruples the power' (2 marks): P is proportional to I squared; so 2 squared = 4 times as much power.
National Grid 4 to 6 mark answers: higher V so lower I for the same P (P = VI), so lower power loss (P = I²R), so less energy wasted as thermal energy and more efficient transmission.
Use the phrase 'rate of energy transfer' for power, and 'thermal energy is dissipated to the surroundings' for waste.
Graph skills: P against I is a curve; P against I² is a straight line through the origin with gradient R. Read off values carefully using the scale.
Check your answer is sensible: household appliances are about 10 W to 3 kW; a kettle current is about 10 A.
**Practical (power of a lamp)**: draw the circuit with the ammeter in series and the voltmeter in parallel across the lamp, then use P = V x I with both readings.

mistakes.r: P = I²R: only the current is squared.
mistakes.w: Writing P = IR² or squaring R

mistakes.r: Convert to watts and amps first: 2.3 kW = 2300 W; 250 mA = 0.25 A.
mistakes.w: Using kW or mA without converting

mistakes.r: Energy is transferred (or dissipated to the surroundings); power is the rate at which this happens.
Power = energy transferred / time. Energy is power x time.
Choose the standard fuse rating just above the normal current, or it will blow during normal use.
mistakes.w: Choosing a fuse equal to or below the normal current

mistakes.r: The wire in the fuse melts when the current is too large, which breaks the circuit.
mistakes.w: Saying a fuse 'stops the electricity getting in'

mistakes.r: At constant current (series) P = I²R rises with R; at constant potential difference (parallel) P = V²/R falls with R.
mistakes.w: Saying more resistance always gives more power

mistakes.r: Doubling the current at constant R makes the power 4 times greater, because P is proportional to I².
mistakes.w: Thinking doubling the current doubles the power

mistakes.r: Give the answer in W (or kW if asked) with working shown.
mistakes.w: Leaving out units or giving the power in the wrong unit

mistakes.r: A voltmeter is connected in parallel across the component; an ammeter is the one that goes in series.
mistakes.w: Connecting the voltmeter in series to measure the potential difference across a lamp.

summary: The specification asks you to recall and use P = VI and P = I²R, to link electrical power to the potential difference across a device and the current in it, and to use these ideas for appliances and fuse choice. It matters because power calculations, fuse selection and the National Grid explanation are common multi-mark Paper 1 questions.

worked.q: A kettle is rated 2.3 kW at 230 V. (a) Calculate the current in the kettle. (b) Which fuse should be fitted: 3 A, 5 A or 13 A? (c) Calculate the resistance of the heating element. [5 marks]
steps: (b) The fuse rating must be above 10 A. 3 A and 5 A would blow in normal use, so use the 13 A fuse.
Check using P = I²R: 10² x 23 = 100 x 23 = 2300 W, which matches.

worked.q: A resistor of 50 ohm carries a current of 0.40 A. (a) Calculate the power transferred. (b) The current is doubled. Calculate the new power and state how it compares. [4 marks]
steps: Compare: 32 / 8.0 = 4, so the power is 4 times larger.

worked.ans: A high potential difference means that, for the same power (P = VI), the current is small. The power wasted in the cables is P = I²R, so a small current causes much less heating of the cables. Less energy is dissipated to the surroundings, so the transmission is more efficient.
worked.q: Explain why the National Grid transmits electricity at a very high potential difference. [4 marks]
steps: Link 1: for a given power, P = VI, so a higher potential difference means a smaller current.
Link 2: the power wasted as heat in the cables is P = I²R.
Link 3: a smaller current greatly reduces the power loss, because it depends on the current squared.
Conclusion: less energy is dissipated as thermal energy to the surroundings, so transmission is more efficient.
